utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Ann Sutherland, together with Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with David Cunningham and Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you. And welcome back, Mr. Ackerman. Are there any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a problem with tomorrow that I've not been able to solve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Anic is not able to be with us tomorrow, and so we have no one to -- with whom we can speak to our client, which is, you know, pretty important during the course of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand. But we'll deal with that. May I ask you: What have you tried to ask from the Registrar, or have you done anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I only learned about the situation over the weekend, so I've not had an opportunity to talk to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Madam Chuqing, please, if you could get hold straight with the office, Ms. Martinez, or whoever it is at the moment, to look into this and to give us information by the next break, so that Mr. Ackerman will be in a position to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Anic will be available for the rest of the week. She just cannot be here on Tuesday, Your Honour. And I'm hoping --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll do something about that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm hoping at some point our new case manager will be able to join us, but it appears that the visa process is grinding slowly, slowly, slowly, and maybe today we'll get some news on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do let me know if there are problems, Mr. Ackerman, so that -- because it's -- sometimes you'll be surprised to hear this, but sometimes we are not informed. So if there is a visa problem, probably we will be the last ones to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't think there's a problem. I think what happened was a significant person departed from the Registrar last week, and the whole thing dropped through the cracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it's back above the cracks again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if there is any way in which we could help, let us know. And I also wanted you to know that in your absence the last two weeks, proceedings went fine, both with Ms. Baruch and Mr. Cunningham, and dealing with -- Ms. Baruch is out now, but Mr. Cunningham, I hope, will be with us until the end of this case. His presence and his participation is not only promising; it's encouraging, and I must congratulate you on your choice. I hope I won't have to go back on my words at some later point in time. But I did want to make this public, because his conduct so far has been exemplary and his expertise is there for everyone to see. So anything from your side, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Just for your information, we shifted all the sittings for this week to this morning. Wednesday we are still sitting in the morning but we are sitting in another courtroom. So Wednesday we will be sitting in Courtroom 2 instead of this courtroom. And there may be the possibility of having to shift also on another day. But that stands to be seen. Can we bring the witness in? Is the witness covered with any --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might just report to you that I filed the response to the Rule 92 bis for the Celinac municipality this morning, so that should be in your hands before the day is out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. If at any time, Mr. Ackerman, you need a short break, let us know. This witness, I understood -- I understand from what Madam Richterova said last Thursday that he's got a problem with his work or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He needs to complete his testimony today. He's due to return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman, let's start with -- have you got a more or less rough guess as to how much time you would require from him on cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'll be handling that witness, and of course it's hard to anticipate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But a rough guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: A rough guess, about 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 45 minutes. So try to make -- to adjust your in-chief, Ms. Sutherland, to -- not to go beyond such time as would leave the Defence without at least -- I still say leave at least an hour, an hour and a quarter for the Defence, because much depends on what he will be testifying in chief in any case. And if there is at any time, Mr. Cunningham, you get an indication as we go along that it is going to involve the Defence in a lengthier cross-examination, please just give me a signal of that so that we will then, if necessary, split the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Accordingly. Okay? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's Witness Number 7.57, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the first time you're giving evidence before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So later on I will explain to you briefly the procedure. In the meantime, what's important for you is to make a solemn declaration that is required of you by our Rules, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. It is the equivalent of an oath in many jurisdictions. Here we give it the form of a solemn declaration. The text is contained in a piece of paper that the usher is just handing to you. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may -- please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I see you're a little bit excited. You don't need to be excited. Please relax. You are not in the lion's den here. You will be treated nicely. And I'll explain to you a little bit before you start what's going to happen. You see the lady on your right, standing up. That's Ms. Sutherland. I suppose you have met her already. She will be putting to you a series of questions, and your duty is to answer each and every question that she puts to you in as fully as -- as fully and as truthfully as you can. That's unless we stop you from answering any question. When she is finished with you, then you will be asked a series of questions by the Defence lawyers, and the Defence lawyers are on your left. And Mr. Cunningham, who is sitting in the centre, will be the person -- the lawyer who will be cross-examining you. I need to advise you here that it's equally your duty to answer each question that is put to you by Mr. Cunningham as truthfully and as fully as you can, as possible, because the accused here has got the right, the fundamental right, to have you cross-examined. Once you are examined by the Prosecution, then he has a right to have questions put to you, and your duty, now that you have entered that solemn declaration, is to speak the truth. If there is a question that you feel you shouldn't answer, then look at me and ask me for permission not to answer it, and I will take due consideration of your submissions and will decide accordingly. Having said that, I leave you in the hands of Ms. Sutherland. You can -- you may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you please state for the record your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Midho Druzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your father's first name is Mahmut?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were born on the 19th of December, 1954, in the town of Bosanski Petrovac, in the Bosanski Petrovac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your ethnicity is Bosniak and your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You grew up in the town of Bosanski Petrovac, where you went to primary school, and then you went to Bihac to attend secondary school, where you completed that in 1972. After that you did your JNA military service in 1973 and 1974?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You need to speak up a little bit for the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You married in 1974 and you have one child?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were employed as a professional driver for the company Sipad Ostrelj in Bosanski Petrovac from 1974 until 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're currently employed as a warden of the centre for refugees from the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long have you held that position?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I've been at this post since 1997, October.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You provided a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2000. When you spoke to the Prosecution yesterday, you were given an opportunity to review that statement, and you wish to make four small corrections to the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If the usher can hand the -- sorry. If we can go through these corrections quickly, because we have a lot to cover in your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you turn to page 6 of your statement, which is in B/C/S, and this is on page 5 of the English, the last paragraph the English and the second paragraph of the B/C/S, the word where it is driven through Drvar should read driven through Bara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, unless this is -- this statement is going to be tendered in evidence, you don't need to go through these corrections. You just put a direct question as you go along. If you need to refer to that particular event, and he will testify accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I'll do it as we testify -- as he testifies, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Druzic, you can put this statement to one side. Have you provided any other signed statement to any authorities in Bosnia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't given a statement to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2000, was based in part on notes that you made in your own personal diary about things that you had experienced during 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And everything you wrote down in this personal diary is of your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the entries in the diary relating to 1992 are described fully in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And there's nothing of relevance that isn't included in your statement that you gave in July 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I wish to turn now to 1990. In that year, you joined the SDA party and elected as a member of the SDA Executive Board in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And in November 1990, you were elected as an SDA representative to the Municipal Assembly and you remained an assemblyman until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you attend any political rallies in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: As far as my direct experience is concerned, I went on an SDS rally which was held in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when the rally was?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I think it was in mid-September.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I think it was either 1990 or 1991. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were the speakers at this rally?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: At this rally were the representatives from Knin. There was Raskovic, Zelenbaba, there were also local people from the SDS. There were also guests from Stara Pazova, from Serbia. But what -- who I remember is Bogdan Kecman, from Kosovo. He was a member of the organisation called Bozur. I remember him well also because of what he said at the rally. I knew him before this because he was a representative of the Sipad company. He had worked in Sipad in Pristina. Because I worked as a driver at the company, transport company in Bosanski Petrovac, and it is very frequently that we transported goods for Serbia and for Kosovo, because the branch office of Sipad was in Kosovo, and its head office was in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the nature of the speeches, and do you recall anything in particular which was said at the rally?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This rally, I was struck by Mr. Bogdan Kecman's speech, when he said if the Muslims do not want to stay with us in Yugoslavia, we will have them impaled, just like the Turks impaled our Serbs at the time when the Turks were ruling. At that moment, I was standing with Dr. Milan Vidovic, and as soon as I heard this word, this speech of his, I immediately left the rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was anybody attending the rally from the SDS republic level?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Up until that time, what was the relationship like between the Bosniaks and the Serbs in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, we lived in a community where there were 22 per cent Muslims, and there were 78 per cent Muslims [as interprete]. Up to that moment, everything was fine, and really I worked in a company where there was a majority of Serbs who were employees. And we worked as a crew of two for each lorry. We were mostly in mixed company, meaning the drivers were -- and I worked with a Serb as a partner, as a driving partner for five years, so that means --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. I know what you're going to say more or less. Yes. We have in the transcript: We lived in a community where there were 22 per cent Muslims and there were 78 per cent Muslims [as interpreted]." So someone got something wrong. Can you repeat how many Muslims --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 78 per cent Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what you wanted to point out, Mr. Ackerman. Yes. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So you were describing how the relationships changed between the Bosniaks and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. From that moment, from that moment, there was separation that started. Serbs to one side, Muslims to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Prior to the war in Croatia in 1991, were there any military units stationed in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was one unit from Ogulin that came to the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac. These were active JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did they come to the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was it before the war in Croatia or after?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I think when there was the withdrawal of the army from the Republic of Croatia, I think that's when they came. But when that exactly was, I wouldn't be able to tell you exactly. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were they stationed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: They were at the police, next to the police there is a military warehouse. That's where they were stationed. And one part was in Bosnaplast, which is a company manufacturing plastic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Prior to the war in Croatia, what television channels were you able to receive?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, we watched Sarajevo TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you able to continue to watch the Sarajevo channel?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know from what time. What happened is that it was turned towards Banja Luka TV, but I can't tell you exactly when that happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "it was turned," do you mean the transmitter?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so from that point on, it was television programmes from Banja Luka TV; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In relation to the radio station in Bosanski Petrovac, did the format change at all; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Already it became national-based. At the time the editor was I think Milan Latinovic. Before that, he had been a teacher. And then he was a headmaster of a school. He then moved to work for the Bosanski Petrovac radio. I think a lot of things changed. The programmes of the radio Bosanski Petrovac changed a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, a lot of things, like the Serb things, they started to grow. There was -- the music changed a lot. Everything became more Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what about the television? What happened in relation to the television?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I didn't watch it much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated earlier that you were employed from 1974 until 1992 as a driver in Sipad Ostrelj company. Can you just tell the Court briefly what the company was about? How many employees did it have?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Sipad Ostrelj was a large company with about 3.500 workers. It was -- it had nine units, that is, these nine units made for that company, Sipad Ostrelj. So there was an administrative services, a door-making plant, Bosanski Petrovac; building, Bosanski Petrovac; sawmill, Krnjeusa, Fana Krnjeusa; and the pellet-making unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was it the largest timber factory in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Why, yes, it was one of the larger companies in Bosnia, insofar as the timber processing is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A lot of people that lived in Bosanski Petrovac municipality were employed at Sipad?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the other main industries or manufacturing organisations in the area, and approximately how many persons did they employ?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: There was Novitet, which is a textile industry, employing about 500, mostly of the female sex. Then Bosnaplast, Bosanski Petrovac, which made plasticware, it employed 100, 150. There was Trgovacki Magazin. That is a trading company with its outlets, employing about 100. Then there was a restaurant business, Hutro Grmec, which also employed a hundred, 150 people. And there were also, of course, private businesses, shops, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did you stop working as a driver for Sipad?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: March or April 1992. March or April.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you voluntarily leave the company?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: We didn't. I was summoned to the company to Autotransport, and my then manager, Dragan Stupar, told me: Midho, give us back the keys. You're not working here as of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many other persons were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: By and large, all the Muslims were fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any Serbs who were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago other industries which had large work forces, Novitet and Bosnaplast are two examples. Were Bosniaks dismissed from these companies too, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I knew about it because my wife worked for the Novitet, the textiles company, and she was dismissed, just as I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: After you were dismissed, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I was at home all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: These other dismissals of persons from the other companies, and also from Sipad, what months were the dismissals occurring? What month or months, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, I know then auto transport, it was March or April 1992. Now, as for other companies, I don't really know, because I didn't really move out or away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: At some point, was there a call to disarm the population?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: May 1992, I'd say. That was when Muslims were called to disarm and hand over their weapons to the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was it only directed to the Muslims, or was it the entire population?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Muslims only.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were you told about this disarming?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: They used an APC to drive around the street and announcing that weapons should be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you obey the direction?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: We did. We went. We, the Muslims, went and turned over our weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: A hunting rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was your house ever searched for weapons after that date?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I think on the 24th or the 25th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any weapons found?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nothing was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened that day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Two cars came, bringing seven or eight policemen and one investigating, one investigating. They came, tied me up, and went over the house. There wasn't any major harassment. My wife wasn't ill-treated. They merely searched the house, they personally, and they also used the detector.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 15th of June, 1992. But after these weapons, I was taken in. I was searched there and I was detained for two days in the police. It was, that is, the 24th and the 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you were taken to the SUP, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. They did that. Where I came, what I was, but then they took me to solitary confinement and kept me there until the next day, until half past 5.00 or 5.00, when they let me go. I wasn't beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were you interrogated by?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, this investigating one, the one who came, Vujo or something. I don't know what his last name is. He comes from Smoljana, and I know that his father was the secretary of the primary school in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did the interrogation last?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Two or three hours, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of questions were you being asked?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Whether Muslims had weapons, whether there were some organisations, who was arming Muslims illegally, and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were kept in solitary cell until around 5.00 the next day. Were you provided with any food or water?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let me tell you: I didn't ask for it, nor did I ask somebody to go and bring it to me. I just somehow managed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were arrested on the 15th of June, 1992. Were you taken to the SUP that day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day we were taken in and brought to the police to give our statements, and that was in the afternoon hours. And no sooner did I go to the door of the police than -- now, of course, I can't remember who it was that was on duty, but turned to the wall, spread your legs, frisked me, and said: You're under arrest. And sent me down to the cellar. And in the cellar they had a kitchen and a canteen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the police station for on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: In the police station, we were detained there until the 1st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever charged with anything?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were being detained there for a fortnight?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you arrived at the police station, you said you went downstairs into the kitchen area. Did you recognise anyone else when you entered the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I did. They were there already, Zijad Ramic, Ekrem Didovic, the late Salih Salimovic, Halil Mesic, Eno Bolic, Emin from Bjelaj. I can't remember his last name. But there were already several other people there, Muslims I mean, detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you interrogated during the fortnight that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't interrogated ever.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you detained within the police station? Was it in the kitchen or was it in another room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: In the canteen, in the cafeteria.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many people were detained in that room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, until the 1st of July, we were about 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of all the people that were detained in the kitchen, in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: All Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how big was the kitchen area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, about 4 by 6, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you provided with any bedding?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No. We slept on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you provided with any blankets?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. We were issued with the army blankets.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you spend the whole fortnight in the canteen area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, for a while. I don't know. I can't remember which policeman was it. But when he was on duty, four or five of us would always be in solitary confinement, isolated from the other people. That is, he would take us away, put us into that cell, and in the morning bring us back. But it was only that one policeman, when he was on duty. But I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was the canteen area crowded with the number of people that were there, or not?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Listen, at that moment, we weren't really thinking about whether it was overcrowded or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened on the 1st of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: At 3.00 in the morning, a policeman on duty came, told us to stand up, collect our belongings, and get out, and we did that. We came out, and there was already a bus parked there to take us on. We had no idea where we were going. After we had all been put in the bus, the bus left off towards Kljuc, that is, via Drvar, and reached the crossroads for Drinca, Bosanski Petrovac, and Bihac, and turned straight, that is, towards Bara, Bukovaca, and Drinic. And when we arrived in Drinic, then we realised we were going to a safe working site, since having worked in a timber company, I knew there was a working site Kozila. And then we reached another junction which forks towards Kozila and towards Vrletina and when it turned left to Kozila, then we were sure we were going to this forest working site, where there were [indiscernible] were housing the administration of that working site.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit P1956.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript reads the buses left off towards Kljuc, that is, via Drvar. Is that one of the things that you wanted to correct in your statement, that it was -- you went via Bara?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's -- that is right. Not through Drvar. You do not need to go through Drvar to go to Kljuc. Drvar is 35 kilometres from Bosanski Petrovac, and goes through the village of Krunic and you cross a hill and come down to Dzevar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, using the pointer, can you point on to the machine to your right and show the Judges the route that you took to get to Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if the audiovisual director could possibly blow up the north-west part of Bosnia, where the witness is pointing. Could you zoom in, please. I think you need to bring the map down on the ELMO machine. Bring the machine out a little bit. Pull the -- bring the -- wheel the machine out a bit so you can take the map down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Can you point to Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just let the map go down a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Pointing again with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All right. Now, follow the road to Kozila from Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Bara, Drinic. So Bara, Drinic, and that's where you go --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how far [Previous translation continues]... From Drinic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: -- to Kozila. About 10 kilometres. All together, about 20 kilometres from Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit for the moment. What time did you arrive at Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: The 1st of July. About an hour later we were already there, at Kozila.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So it was around 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes. It was very early.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: The bus fetched up below the shacks where we would be put up later on, and a guy came out, dark-haired, curly hair, with a beard, and told us to line up. So the 30 of us lined up, and he told us to put aside our personal belongings, to take off any watches we might have, or chains, or whatever, wallets and the like. And after we had done that, we started entering the shack, the wooden shed, in the order in which we had been lined up. Let me say: There were two shacks. One of them, where we were accommodated, was surrounded with barbed wire, and it was about 2 metres tall. And there was only one entrance, and we used it to enter. And from the lower side, that is, to the north of the shack -- of course, one wants to see everything, so I spotted immediately a machine-gun nest with two soldiers there, with two guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How many machine-gun nests were there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No. We saw this one when we arrived, but we could see that same machine-gun nest after we had been put in the shack because through the opening which was about one centimetre, one could see outside. Because that place, I mean the place where the machine-gun was, our window was right across it, so that we could watch it from inside the shack. How many of them there were, I really don't know, because that was all the that I could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say there was an opening of about one centimetre, is this on the windows of the buildings that you were placed into?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I know well the working sites, because I used to work for that company. Before the war, I worked for forestry unit, in 1974. I used to drive heavy-duty vehicle, and I frequently drove foremen out to that working site. Those shacks were very well made.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were the windows boarded up in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: From the inside, the windows had been removed; and from the outside, there was a grille made of boards, of lathes [phoen]. That is, they had completely shut the windows, having left only about one-centimetre cracks so that some light might get in, and some air too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at two sketches, hand-drawn sketches that were drawn by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if the witness could also be given the photographs, Exhibit P1864.1 to P1864.8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, looking first at the sketch marked MD-A, was this sketch drawn by you when you gave your statement in July 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Does your signature appear anywhere on that sketch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, can the sketch be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that we make sure that we are looking at the same one? Please. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, does your signature appear anywhere on that document; and if so, can you point with the pointer on the machine to your right.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if that could be provisionally marked as P1891.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Would you put the next sketch, marked MD-B, on the ELMO. Was that sketch also hand drawn by you when you gave your statement in July 2000?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And can you point [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can that document be provisionally marked P1891.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham, I'm admitting these two documents, taking it that there is no objection on your part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you put the first drawing now, which is P1891.1, on the ELMO. Can you take the pointer and point to where the building where you were taken when you first came off the bus?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is pointing at the space immediately in front of what is indicated as Baraka 1 on the sketch. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was just about to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you now take the first photograph, which is marked P1864.1, and it has the ERN number 0214-1401. What is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: You can see the well, where horses would be taken to drink water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is the Kozila camp -- would the Kozila camp be in the foreground or in the distance of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: The Kozila camp is before this, on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you look at photograph number P1864.3, which is 0214-1402. Not that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's .2. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is .3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now this is .2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what is that a photo of?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: On this photograph, I can see the hut where I was. Here these tree trunks, that was not there in 1992, when we were detained. So where this timber is, and this wooden hut next to it, that wasn't there. But what I am showing, pointing to, the house, the hut where we were, that's where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the white building, and that is the one that's marked on your sketch MD-A as Baraka 1?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we have the next photograph, P1864.2, which is 0214-1398.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That is stables. That's opposite the shacks, on the other side of the road. This is where the horses were. These were horses that were --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so that is a --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... These were the horses that were kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That is a continuation of the road that we just saw in the previous photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This is the continuation of the road which goes to Bosanski Petrovac, and on the first photograph, where I pointed to the well, that's the road which goes to the opposite direction, which goes towards --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Just put --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Srnac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just put MD-A back on the ELMO and point out the stables which are in that photograph and the well which was in the first photograph that I showed you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: It was here. So this is the road which goes back to Bosanski Petrovac. And where the well is, that's in the opposite direction, going towards Srnac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So as we look at the sketch, the stables are in the bottom right-hand corner of the diagram, and the well is on the bottom left-hand corner of the diagram?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: While we have that sketch on the ELMO, can you please point to where the commander's office was.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're now pointing to the -- on the sketch to the building marked Kancelarija?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, office. Here, before the camp was established, this is where the chief of the construction site was, and his personnel were there in these offices. That was the facility which was supposed to be for the director and the head of the construction site, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And of the three photos we've just looked at, the office doesn't appear in any one of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you also, while we have this sketch on the ELMO, point to the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the building directly above the office?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The building to the -- above and to the right of the kitchen, what was in that building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I think that was a blacksmith's.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the building above and to the left of the kitchen, what was in that building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Most probably a warehouse, a storage space.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can just put photograph number P1864.3 back on the ELMO, which was the second photograph, which is 0214-1402. And point again to the barrack -- the Baraka 1, which is on your sketch. And the building right next door to that --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- The wooden building, was that there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No. No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the photograph number P1864.4, which is 0214-1399, be placed on ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, pointing to the room that is marked Baraka 1 on your sketch, pointing in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The building which you sketched as the kitchen, can you point on this photograph where that is.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the building with the -- it looks like a white truck is parked.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the barbed wire, can you just point on that photograph where the barbed wire was.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that clear for Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you now be shown the second sketch that you drew, MD-B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can that be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We will go into detail shortly about the different rooms, but can you just explain what's in this diagram.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This is a sketch. This is the position of the rooms in the shack where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the marking, is it SOB.1, means room number 1, room number 2, room number 3, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you point, while we have this diagram, where the toilet facilities were.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is marked with "WC." The room directly next to that, what was in that room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This was a pantry, so when people were in this shack, they would leave the tools there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was it used for during the time that you were detained in Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: For a while, Zika Ramic and later Saban Spahic and myself, we spent some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is the room you referred to as the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. To start with, there was Zika Ramic there by himself, and then Saban Spahic joined him. And then later on from room number 6, which was also solitary confinement, I went into this pantry or storage space.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that -- you have marked that -- is it Ostava?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the room across from the toilet facilities, where you have marked "KUP," [Realtime transcrip read in error "CUP"] what was in that room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's bathroom, Kupatilo. That's where the showers were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And while we are at it, may have misunderstood myself, but between this room that he's just indicated and KUP 1, there is the top-left corner of outside KUP 1, a small box, and then there is the Dezurni Policajac. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Here. While we were detained in the shack, there was a table and a chair, where there was the duty policeman 24 hours on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And for the record, my attention is being drawn in the transcript, the shower room or whatever it's called, it's K-U-P on the document and not C-U-P. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think you may proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could photograph number P1864.8, which is ERN 0214-1394, be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, what's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: You can see shack number 1, where we were detained, and next to it was shack number 2, which was made of timber.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: As you're looking at the photograph, the white building, that is what you call shack number 1? And shack number 2 is behind shack number 1, and you cannot see it in this photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Here it is. Here it is, shack number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I've got the photo -- the -- yes. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Shack number 1, if you look carefully at the photo, is further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. So it's basically where you want to see the right perspective, you have to go behind shack number 1 to understand the layout of this photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was getting confused with another photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, can you point on the photograph that's on the ELMO to rooms 4, 5, and 6, that you have marked on your sketch MD-B.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please place photograph number P1864.7, which is ERN 0214-1393, on the ELMO. What's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Shack number 1. And what you can see down there, that was not there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's the wooden building to the right of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Further down, that second shack was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what are the room numbers in this photograph which correspond to your sketch?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Number 4, and part of the window of room number 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just for completeness, Your Honour, because they have been tendered, if the witness can be -- the photograph number P1864.6, which is ERN number 0214-1392, that photograph could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This is part of the shack, facing shack number 1, and this is where you would enter the kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that's the kitchen building?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And finally, P1864.5, which is 0214-1397. What's shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: The kitchen is here, and this part where you can see the steps, that's the part facing the shack, where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with those photographs and sketches. Mr. Druzic, who was in charge of the camp?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Miso Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you know this?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: When we were detained in the rooms, this is the person who was there to meet us when we came to the Kozila camp. He entered our room and introduced himself, said he was Miso Zoric and that he was the one in charge of the Kozila camp, that he was the head of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you know him before?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you told by the other detainees where he worked previously?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Later on. Later on we found out that some people knew him, some Bosniaks, some Muslims, and it was said that he had worked as a guard in the Luka prison in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were any other persons brought to Kozila that day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening hours, another bus arrived, also a bus load of Bosniaks, who were taken to the police station, and in the evening were brought to the Kozila camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're referring to the police station in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there another group of people that were brought to the camp earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Before we arrived, there were already people there who were brought from Prekaja, from Drvar. There was a group of 18 people from Orasac and Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So by the end of the day, approximately how many people were in Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: About 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown exhibit P1840, which is the list of persons. If the English could be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, do you see your name listed there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, under number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And is that your first name?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: My name is Midho Druzic, not Midhat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But given that it says Midhat Druzic, otherwise known as Midho, you're assuming that they're referring to you at number 9?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: My name is the one that I was given by my late father and mother, not a name that I was given by someone else. My first name is Midho, M-i-d-h-o, not Midhat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: All these names listed 1 to 30, were they all brought with you on the bus in the early hours of the 1st of July to Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, how many families in Bosanski Petrovac had that name Druzic, that you know of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How many families in Bosanski Petrovac had that surname, Druzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are one of the most -- the strongest tribes, as far as Bosniaks are concerned, in that area. It's very large family of Druzic people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was there anyone in Bosanski Petrovac with the family name Druzic that was called Midhat, that you know of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You exclude it or you simply don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly not. I rule out that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Ms. Sutherland, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. Instead of "tribe," "clan" would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The professions of these people are quite varied, are they not?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: A number of them have private businesses, their own private businesses?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For example, the person listed at number 1, the person listed at number 13, 16, 18, 24. There is an economist there listed at number 8. Is that correct? There's a legal officer --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Hidic, Muharem, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's a legal officer at number 15?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There's a painter at number 20, a locksmith at number 22; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Osman Hadzic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, turning to the second page of that document, it states that the date of this document is the 2nd of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: They were brought on the 1st, in the evening, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that was the group that you referred to a moment ago when you said that they were taken to the SUP and in Bosanski Petrovac, and then they were brought to Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes. They were taken off the road, collected, rounded up, and then they were brought, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document, unless Your Honour has any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sir, how long were you detained at Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of July until the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So that would be approximately seven weeks?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, 36 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court the conditions in the camp during your detention? And by that I mean were you given adequate food and water, your sleeping conditions, the personal hygiene?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: We were in rooms, in shacks, and it depended on who was where. I think in our room number 1 there were about 18 of us. We slept on sponges and we would have a blanket to cover ourselves. As far as toilet facilities are concerned, we had a bucket in the corner that was used as a toilet, and we received water in cannisters that we used during the day. While I was in the camp from the 1st of July until the 6th of August, I didn't go out to the toilet to relieve myself, or did I go to the showers. Whatever I did, I did in the room where I slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was that because you didn't want to or you weren't allowed to go to the toilets or the showers?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I avoided being noticed more than anything, so I just tried to keep quiet, keep a low profile, be in my room, sit down or lie down, and just not to be noticed by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you given the opportunity for daily exercise?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: No. No. For that -- during that time, while I was at the Kozila camp, it was only once that we were taken out for a walk, from 11.00 or 12.00, one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And was that within the confines of the camp or was that outside?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That was within the compound, within the compound of the camp, inside the wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you physically mistreated whilst you were detained in Kozila?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was. On a couple of occasions I was physically mistreated, humiliated, by the guards, who were in the Kozila camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many times did this happen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Five or six times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to take you now through each of the times that you were beaten or that you were physically mistreated. How long --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to start that after the break or do you want to start now? You've got three minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We could perhaps have an early break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. So we'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's tackle the first problem. The interpreter business has been taken care of. Hopefully we should get some kind of confirmation pretty soon. What volume of documents are we talking about, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's four binders, four or five binders, some large -- one or two small, one or two large. I think -- how many are there? There are two in the back and there are -- I think there are two or three here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is the real problem? Has he been told that he cannot take them with him or that they are not prepared to carry them for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The guard told me that the police who do the transport will not let him take anything that he didn't bring to Court. They won't let him take anything back with him that he didn't bring here. And this is a brand new problem. I mean, we've given him stuff and he's taken it back from the beginning of the trial. Just all of a sudden today there seems to be a new rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Chuqing, will you handle that as well, please? Okay. Thank you. We'll see into that, because if it's -- the police refusing to carry them for him is one thing, and not allowing him to take them with him simply because he did not bring them over is another matter. So we'll look into that and hopefully within the next few minutes we should come back to you on it. Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Let's go through the beatings. If it's -- I suggest to you move fast on these. If it's -- if necessary, I will even authorise you to read straight from his statement and ask him whether he confirms what's written there. Because there is a lot of details about each and every beating, and others that were also beaten. So choose whichever way you like, but please do keep in mind that we need a good hour left to be left for Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Druzic, just before we broke, I asked you approximately how many times you had been beaten, and then I said that we were going to go through in some detail each of these beatings. How long had you been at Kozila when you were first mistreated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, one moment. Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Cunningham, if -- and I see that your interpreter is not present in the room. If at any time you need to -- yes, but -- if at any time you need to consult with your client or your client needs to consult with you and you feel it is necessary to stop the sitting, we will stop the sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. She will be back in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She worked throughout the break and so we've told her she can take a short break and she'll be back quite soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that causes you a problem at any time, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Ms. Sutherland, I'm sure you appreciate that. Yes, Mr. Druzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long had you been at Kozila before you were first mistreated?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: How long was I there before they started interrogating me, you mean, ill-treating me? Five days. They took me in on the sixth day, the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Court how you were called out and where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: As you know from the sketches, there was a guard in the shack, on duty there. Around 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening, he called out Zika Ramic, who was also in dormitory 1. And 20 minutes later, Zika returned and my name was called out. I went out, and the duty guard outside took me to that office where the Kozila administration -- Kozila camp administration was. And that guard who escorted me was called Zeljko Brankovic. A year or so earlier, he ran Dzakarta tavern, so that I knew that he came from Rasovac. But I've never had any personal communication with him. And no sooner did he take me into that room where the administration was and where I recognised Miso Zoric than this Brankovic hit me with his baton on the head. And I lost consciousness. And when I came to again, when I came to again, I was sitting in a chair. I saw Miso Zoric, and a few guys around him, those who were guarding, I mean who were guards in the camp. The interrogation started straight away. That I was a Mujahedin, that I was a balija. They were saying: Tell us, who is the organiser? Who is the leader of the Muslims? Where are your weapons? And that was the general drift of it. And then he put me up and took me into a corner. When he was the first one to start slapping me in the face and beating me. So it lasted for a while, and then a big man, a blond one, a policeman, who I didn't know then. Later on I found out what he was, but his name was Milan --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just pause there. You said he was the first one to stand up and start slapping me in the face. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Miso Zoric. Miso Zoric. And after him, a fair-haired, big guy came up to me and hit me in the lower part of my body, so that I fell down. And then they started kicking me with their feet or whatever they had, those, I mean, men who were with Zoric in that same office. It lasted not less than one hour. And that same guy who had brought me into that office with the administration of the camp, he was also the one who took me back to the shack, to my room number 1. I was beaten on the head, on the back, and the next day I felt severe pain in my legs. I suppose it was due to these blows with their boots.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were you kicked in the genital area at all during this beating?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: This one, Milan Knezevic, yes, he kicked me there after the first blows that were inflicted by Zoric.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned Miso Zoric, the commander of the camp, who was interrogating you and who also struck some blows to your body. You mentioned the name of Zeljko Brankovic, one of the guards who brought you to the commander's office, and you just mentioned Milan Knezevic. Can you name the other guards who were in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, I learnt who they were later, so that it was later on that I found out their names. One of them was Glusica, who also worked as a prison guard at Luka, in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you name the other --

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Salasa, Zoran Salasa, who is the -- an in-law of Miso Zoric's. Filipovic, whose nickname was Rudi because he worked in Rudi's shop in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Nine Puzigaca?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nine Puzigaca, yes, I know him. He was a locksmith and we worked together at Autotransport and we were good acquaintances before that. He used to live and still lives in Drinic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Neno Latinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Miro Latinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Nedjo, I'm sorry, Latinovic.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Nedjo, Nedjo Latinovic. Yes. I began to know him in the camp. I didn't know him before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was he in the room that night?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was, Nedjo Latinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Milan Kresoja?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Milan Kresoje. Yes. He was there. He used to work at the police administration in Bihac before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that after the beating that night that you couldn't walk the following day.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many days after this first beating before you were mistreated again?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Seven days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court what happened on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Same thing. A guard comes, calls me out, escorts me, and the leader in all the ill-treatings that I suffered was Miso Zoric, who would always be the one who would start it, that is, first provocation, and then beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You were called out to his office this night?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he was interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Same thing: Interrogated and then just the same thing as the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise the guards that were in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. Same. It was the same group of people who beat us -- no, not us; me, who beat me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did Miso Zoric have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: He did. He had a bayonet, with four S's, and forced me to kiss it. I refused to do that. And he hit me here and cut me. You can still see it. Whether he wanted to do or not, but I started bleeding. Why should I kiss four S's?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're pointing to under your chin?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did he cut the skin?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Here. Yes. I bled here. You can see the scar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: After that, when I was taken back to the shack, I wasn't taken to room 1, and they put me in room 6, alone, because it was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did that beating last before they took you to room number 6?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Well, it was -- as a rule, it was half an hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How long did you stay in room number 6?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Again, I was called out from room 6 three days later. But before me, from the room next to me, that is, room 3, Saban Spahic was called out, around 3.00 in the morning. Saban was taken away and then half an hour later, my name is called out and I was taken there. As I was entering that office where they -- this camp command was, we bypassed each other in the doorway, that is, Saban was coming out and I was coming in. Miso Zoric was yelling and telling the guard: Kill him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're referring to Spahic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Spahic, yes. As the guard was taking him out. So I was brought in and I saw that desk where the Saban Spahic had been sitting was all covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just pause there.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Miso Zoric --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you see him -- you said that you saw him as you were entering the building and he was walking out. What was his condition?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. You're right. I saw him as he was coming out. One could see on his face that he had been beaten on his face. You can you could see --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And after you heard Zoric say: Take him away and kill him, what happened then when you entered the room?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: I was ordered to sit at that table at that desk where Saban Spahic had been sitting, and the whole table was covered with blood, and Miso Zoric ordered me to lick it up. I wouldn't -- I didn't want to do it, and he grabbed me by the hair and used my face to wipe the table. That was all bloody. After that, Salasa ordered me to take off my fur jacket and my shirt, that is, to strip myself to the waist, and I did that. I put those things next to the chair on which I was sitting and then I was ordered it put my hands at my back and my face down on the table, and the beating started with the baton from the kidneys to here, behind the head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript fur jacket. We are in July here. Are we sure we had a good translation? Because in the statement that is referred to as a sweater. So perhaps you can tell us what you were wearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a white jacket and a sweater. But when they beat us, we put more things on, so that it hurts you less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just before you continue with the beating that you were talking about with Zoran Salasa. Prior to that, when Miso Zoric was making you -- ordering you to lick Saban Spahic's blood on the table, what was he saying to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Cursing. There were always curses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What sort of curses was he saying?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO DRUZIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, the first one, cursing at Turkish mothers. There was mention of Mujahedin and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
